subject: lonomia caterpillar
title: Brushing This Caterpillar Can Stop Your Blood From Clotting

scenes.text: One touch of this caterpillar can stop your blood clotting.
Lonomia obliqua, southern Brazil. About 2 inches long, bark-brown, bristling with hollow spines, resting on tree trunks in groups of dozens.
Lean on the trunk and the spines break off in your skin. At first it feels like a burn. Then it fades.
Hours later the venom switches off your clotting system. Bruises spread, gums bleed, and in the worst cases the bleeding reaches the brain.
In the 1990s, hundreds of people a year were stung in one Brazilian state. Until an antivenom arrived in 1996, around 2 percent of them died.
The antidote exists now. The caterpillar still looks exactly like bark.

description:
A caterpillar in southern Brazil carries venom that stops human blood from clotting.
Lonomia obliqua larvae rest in groups on tree trunks and look like bark. Their hollow spines deliver toxins that break down fibrinogen and trigger a bleeding syndrome, with bruising, gum bleeding and, in severe cases, brain haemorrhage or kidney failure. Hundreds of accidents a year were reported in Rio Grande do Sul in the 1990s, with a death rate of roughly 2 percent before the Butantan Institute's antivenom became available in 1996.
Which harmless-looking animal would you least want to touch?
first_comment: The same venom is being studied as a medicine, because anything that controls clotting that precisely is useful. Which deadly animal has a hidden upside?
